hero.subtitle: A fall in a Weed storefront, parking lot, or rental can turn a routine day upside down. We handle premises liability claims in Siskiyou County and understand how California law builds these cases.

about.title: Weed Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Weed is a small place, home to about 2,556 people, and a fall here often happens somewhere familiar: a market along S Weed Boulevard, a gas station off the Rt 97 junction, a motel parking lot near the I-5 exits, or a rental where the porch step gave way. Ice and packed snow on walkways, meltwater tracked into entryways, and dim lighting on early evenings are common ways people in Siskiyou County end up on the ground. California premises liability turns on notice. You generally must show the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and did not repair it or warn you. The days right after a fall matter. Photographs of the spot, the names of anyone who saw it, and a prompt written request that the business hold its surveillance footage can make the difference later. We handle premises liability claims on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.title: Notice Is the Heart of the Case
items.desc: California requires proof that the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. Our team knows how to pin down how long a spill, ice patch, or broken step had been there and who was responsible for checking it.

items.title: Deadlines That Can Sneak Up
items.desc: Most premises claims in California must be filed within two years, but if the property belongs to a city, county, or other public entity, the window to act is much shorter. Getting started early keeps those options open.

items.title: Fault Is Not All-or-Nothing
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, so even if an owner argues you were partly distracted or wearing the wrong shoes, a claim is not automatically lost. Your recovery is simply reduced by your share, which we will push back on with evidence.

items.question: I slipped on ice outside a business on S Weed Boulevard. Is the owner responsible?
items.answer: It depends on what the owner knew and what they did about it. If ice had built up over hours or days and nothing was done to clear, salt, or warn about it, that can support a notice argument under California law. Weather alone does not settle the question, so photos of the conditions and the time of your fall help us evaluate it.

items.question: How do I get the store's surveillance video before it disappears?
items.answer: Many businesses overwrite footage within days or weeks, so speed matters. Send a short written request to the owner or manager asking them to preserve all video from the date and time of your fall, and keep a copy. Our team can follow up with a formal preservation letter, but your early request creates a record that the footage was asked for.
